questions.q: Why plan capacity for the peak and not for the mean?
options: Failures happen when demand exceeds capacity, which happens at peaks
why: Peaks are usually harder to forecast.
Correct: the system fails at the peak, not on average.
The mean is not zero.
Peaks cost more to serve.

questions.q: Peak forecast 6 000 rps, headroom adds 15%, one server handles 400 rps, target utilisation 75%. How many servers (round up)?
Your 90th-percentile ETA is checked on 2 000 orders and 1 500 arrive before it. What is the coverage and what does it mean?
options: 75%: the quantile is too low, too many late orders
why: Correct: 1 500/2 000 = 75%, but it should be near 90%. The predicted quantile is too small.
A perfect model has coverage near 90%.
The coverage is 75%, not 90%.
25% is the share of late orders, not the coverage.

questions.q: Which features are valid for an ETA model at order time? (pick all)
options: Restaurant prep time over the last hour
The actual delivery time of this order
Weather forecast issued before the order
why: Known before the order.
That is the target, leakage.
Known at prediction time.
Known before the order.

questions.q: Scenario: servers take 3 months to buy and install. You forecast usage with MAE of 3% at 1 week and 14% at 12 weeks. Which error should drive the headroom?
options: The 12-week error, because the decision is made 12 weeks ahead
why: That horizon is too short for the decision.
Correct: use the uncertainty at the lead time of the decision.
The average hides the decision horizon.
Headroom must come from the forecast error.

questions.q: Scenario: customers complain about late deliveries, but your mean ETA error is small. What do you check?
options: The error tail (P90/P95) and bias by segment, and the calibration of the promised quantile
why: The mean hides a long tail of late orders.
Correct: late deliveries are in the tail and in some segments.
R-squared does not show tail errors.
MAPE does not address the tail.
